kernelIdea: |z| = √(a² + b²) is the distance from 0; |z| = √(z z̄); it is the absolute value, extended from ℝ to ℂ; |z − w| is the distance between z and w, and |z − w| = r describes a circle.

kernels.l1: How far from home? Measure it with a piece of string.
kernels.l2: To find how far a spot is from the start, use the across part and the up part and make a right triangle. The slanted side is the distance.
kernels.l3: The absolute value |z| is the distance from 0 to z, and Pythagoras gives |a + bi| = √(a² + b²). For ordinary numbers it is just the usual distance from zero.
kernels.l4: The absolute value of a complex number is its straight-line distance from the origin, found from the two parts by the right-triangle rule. It agrees with absolute value on the number line, and the distance between two complex numbers describes circles.
kernels.l5: The absolute value is straight-line distance to the origin. Distances, circles and discs are all described by inequalities in the distance between two complex numbers.
kernels.l6: The absolute value is the distance from a complex number to the origin. It multiplies through products and obeys the triangle inequality, so it measures distance exactly the way length does in coordinate geometry.
kernels.l7: The absolute value is the straight-line distance from the origin. It extends absolute value on the number line, multiplies through products, obeys the triangle inequality, and turns a fixed distance into a circle.
kernels.l8: Modulus is the norm making ℂ a complete normed field; multiplicativity is the norm of the quadratic extension, and completeness is what makes complex analysis possible.
